doc.title: Scott Robinson interviewed by Monk Rowe,Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

title: Teaching at Berklee and the music college disease
summary: He briefly taught there, including tenor history, and complains students would rather play scales than listen.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: And you went on to be a faculty member there.
For about a year and a half, a part timer.
Um hum, teaching ensembles and instrument repair, and the history of tenor saxophone styles.
Wow. Were the students, did you try to get the students to play styles like that or was it mostly a listening thing.

No it was a listening, it was a lecture class. It was listening and history, and identifying records, identifying players, stuff like that. It was hard because these people for the most part never heard of Chu Berry or — maybe they knew Lester Young and they probably knew the name Ben Webster but had never heard him play. Really. Tenor players even. So it was kind of a struggle. I had to say listen for this type of sound and this way of turning a phrase around, and then I would quiz them by playing records, to try to get them to identify the players. It was difficult. There were very few that really wanted to go home and listen on their own and find out what was really going on with the instrument. You know most young music students, they just want to play as much stuff on the horn as they can, you know, I don’t have time to sit for hours and listen to Lester Young and Chu Berry, I’ve got to get the horn out and play all these scales and chords as fast as I can. That’s the disease. that’s the music college disease. So I was happy to play my tiny role in attempting to alleviate that particular affliction.

I haven’t quite heard it put like that but I know what you’re saying, and some people have echoed that as far as the jazz education and how it trains players — the fact that there’s not all the opportunities to play that there used to be I guess is a little hard to overcome, don’t you think?
